newsitem.title: USA: Agency protects coho salmon in central California.
newsitem.headline: Agency protects coho salmon in central California.

text.p: The National Marine Fisheries Service said Friday it was protecting the dwindling central California coho salmon by listing the fish as a threatened species under the Endangered Species Act.

The service said it was deferring by six months a decision on whether to list two other coho salmon populations found in northern California and Oregon because of substantial scientific disagreement about their numbers and potential threats to their existence.
The agency's decision to postpone action on these two populations was denounced by environmental groups. Some accused the agency of deferring to timber industry politics.

"By allowing timber companies to continue logging at unsustainable rates and destroying coho salmon habitat, the National Marine Fisheries Service is choosing to let this majestic species go extinct," Sierra Club official Elyssa Rosen said in a statement.

"It's very disappointing. We don't think that there really is a significant scientific disagreement about the need for listing the Coho in northern California and Oregon," said Michael Anderson, Wilderness Society resource analyst in Portland, Oregon. "It far more smacks of a political desire to accommodate the state agencies in Oregon and California..."
Environmental groups petitioned the Fisheries Service two years ago to protect the coho salmon and the Fisheries Service was under federal court order to make a decision by Friday.

Fisheries Service spokesman Brian Gorman said it was clear that the central California coho salmon were in "dire straits". Their numbers had fallen from 100,000 in the 1940s to about 6,000 adults that were now returning each year to spawning streams. "That's enough to make anybody sit up and take notice," he said.

But the Fisheries Service said it needed more time to gather information and resolve conflicting data before it could make a final decision on the two other coho salmon populations in northern California and Oregon.

The decision, which was eagerly awaited by environmentalists and officials in California and Oregon, was seen as highly sensitive in an election year. Once a species is listed under the Endangered Species Act, industrial activity, development and water usage that could harm its habitat are closely scrutinized by the authorities.

California Gov. Pete Wilson, a Republican, urged President Clinton Thursday to delay listing the coho salmon, saying it could lead to "a virtual shutdown of logging, mining, ranching and other agricultural activity over large parts of California." Oregon Gov. John Kitzhaber, a Democrat, had also asked the Fisheries Service to delay a decision.

Environmentalists had hoped that a listing of the northern California coho salmon would provide protection for the Headwaters Forest, an ancient redwood forest which has been at the center of a long battle between environmentalists and the timber industry.

Fisheries service scientists said the coho's decline in California was caused by habitat degradation from logging, farming, flood control, mining, urbanization and hatchery practices as well as drought and poor ocean conditions.

Hilda Diaz-Soltero, Fisheries Service Southwest regional administrator, said federal agencies would work closely with government officials, private landowners, fishermen and environmental organizations on conservation measures to restore the coho salmon in the region.
